name: Stanford Canaries in the Coal Mine and August 2026 update
citation: Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, Ruyu Chen. 'Canaries in the Coal Mine? Six Facts about the Recent Employment Effects of Artificial Intelligence.' Stanford Digital Economy Lab working paper. Three vintages: (1) 26 August 2025, 57 pages; (2) 13 November 2025, 65 pages; (3) 'August 2026' revision released 12 August 2026, 140 pages, https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/app/uploads/2026/08/Canaries_August2026.pdf. Accompanying lab post: 'No Widespread Displacement, but the AI Employment Gap for Young Workers Has Widened to 19%', Stanford Digital Economy Lab, 12 August 2026, https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/news/canariesaug26/. Publication page: https://digitaleconomy.stanford.edu/publications/canaries-in-the-coal-mine/. Note: the old 2025 PDF URLs now 301-redirect to the August 2026 PDF, so the 2025 texts are only reachable through the Wayback Machine (the lab says earlier versions are available on request).
source_tier: Working paper (not peer-reviewed in any of its three vintages) plus the lab's own news post summarising it. Uses proprietary ADP payroll data.
access_status: Fully read for the purposes of this note: August 2026 PDF (abstract, introduction, Facts 1 to 6, robustness, Sections 4 and 5, discussion, Appendix K and L, software-developer passages) and the 12 August 2026 news post in full. August 2025 and November 2025 PDFs opened via Wayback Machine snapshots (abstract, Fact 1, within-firm regression passage, conclusion). Figures in the appendices were read only as captions; values were not read off charts.
author_credentials: Economists at Stanford. Brynjolfsson: Jerry Yang and Akiko Yamazaki Professor, Senior Fellow at Stanford HAI, Director of the Stanford Digital Economy Lab, NBER research associate. Chandar: labour economist, Research Director for AI Economics and Policy at the lab. Chen: Stanford. Interests to note: the data come from ADP, a commercial payroll provider that granted access (2025 versions: 'We are grateful to ADP for access to the data and the Stanford Digital Economy Lab for financial support'); one of the two main exposure measures is Anthropic's Economic Index. No commercial stake in the finding itself is declared in the passages read.

exact_quotes.quote: employment of young workers (ages 22–25) in AI-exposed occupations now stands 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with that of their less-exposed peers; experienced workers show no comparable gap.

Earlier versions of this study headlined regression estimates adjusting for firm-level shocks (a 13% relative decline as of July 2025 data; 16% as of September 2025 data). We now emphasize the simpler descriptive divergence, which requires no modeling choices: by this same measure, the kept-pace shortfall was 15% at the July 2025 data vintage and has since widened to 19% as of June 2026.

Employment of 22–25-year-olds in the two most exposed quintiles fell about 11% between November 2022 and June 2026, while employment of the same age group in the three least-exposed quintiles grew about 10%—a divergence of 21 percentage points, or 19% relative to growth for the bottom three quintiles.

We find no evidence that increased separations explain the divergence between more- and less-exposed young workers. Separation rates fell for both groups and, among young workers, fell at least as much in the most exposed occupations as in the least exposed, the opposite of what displacement would imply. The divergence instead reflects hiring, with the gap in hiring rates between more- and less-exposed young workers opening after 2022.
We caution that these quantities are determined in equilibrium, with changes in firms' hiring potentially a function of workers' exit rates and vice versa.

We caution that this work does not estimate a causal impact of AI: these are descriptive facts, and ongoing work is needed to determine how much they are caused by the spread of generative AI rather than merely correlated with it.
We interpret these facts as early, descriptive indicators—canaries in the coal mine—rather than causal estimates

These are descriptive patterns, not causal estimates of the effect of AI. The timing and structure of the changes are suggestive, but the data alone cannot establish how much of the divergence was caused by generative AI rather than other forces affecting the labor market.
Is AI causing these changes? We cannot yet answer that question definitively.
we do not view this paper—or any single study—as definitive evidence of AI's labor-market effects.
Taken together, the magnitude of the divergence appears specific to the ADP sample, but its direction is consistent.

Holding the specification fixed, the fourth-quintile estimate is therefore stable across vintages, while the estimate for the most exposed quintile attenuates and is no longer statistically significant.
exact_quotes.location: August 2026 PDF, Online Appendix L, p.140

exact_quotes.quote: By July, 2025, employment for software developers aged 22-25 declined by nearly 20% compared to its peak in late 2022.
By September 2025, employment for software developers aged 22-25 declined nearly 20% compared to its peak in late 2022.
early-career workers (ages 22-25) in the most AI-exposed occupations have experienced a 13 percent relative decline in employment even after controlling for firm-level shocks.
Early-career workers (ages 22-25) in AI-exposed occupations experienced 16% relative employment declines, controlling for firm-level shocks, while employment for experienced workers remained stable.

While our main estimates may be influenced by factors other than generative AI, our results are consistent with the hypothesis that generative AI has begun to significantly affect entry-level employment.
This slowdown in hiring at the entry level provides early suggestions that generative AI may be affecting the career ladder in the American labor market.

key_claims: August 2026 revision, six facts in the authors' terms: (1) no evidence of widespread, economy-wide job displacement from AI; (2) employment of 22 to 25 year olds in AI-exposed occupations is 19% below where it would be had it kept pace with less-exposed peers, with no comparable gap for experienced workers; (3) the divergence has widened steadily since August 2025; (4) it operates primarily through reduced hiring rather than increased separations; (5) declines are concentrated where AI usage substitutes for human tasks, while complementary usage goes with flat or rising employment, especially for experienced workers; (6) adjustment is through employment rather than base compensation. New mechanism material: young-worker declines are in codified-knowledge occupations, experienced-worker gains in tacit-knowledge occupations; women are more exposed on average. The six facts are NOT the same list as in 2025. The 2025 versions' six facts were: declines for early-career workers in exposed occupations such as software development and customer support; overall employment still growing but stagnant for the young; declines in automating not augmenting uses; a 13% (later 16%) relative decline after firm-time effects; adjustment in employment more than pay; robustness to remote work and sample choices. The hiring-versus-separations fact and the explicit 'no economy-wide displacement' fact are new in 2026. The 2026 tone on causality is more guarded than 2025's 'consistent with the hypothesis that generative AI has begun to significantly affect entry-level employment'.

sample_and_method: Observational, descriptive. Anonymised administrative payroll records from ADP (which serves firms employing over 26 million US workers). Analysis sample is a balanced panel of firms observed monthly from January 2021 to June 2026, 3.5 to 5 million employees a month; an extended panel runs from January 2018. Full-time workers under 70 with positive earnings. Job titles mapped to 2010 SOC codes; titles are missing for roughly 30% of the sample and are imputed from the worker's own history in the 2026 version. Occupations sorted into AI exposure quintiles using Eloundou et al. (2024) GPT-4 beta scores and the Anthropic Economic Index (automative versus augmentative Claude usage), with five alternative measures as checks. Outcomes compared by age band (22-25, 26-30, 31-34, 35-40, 41-49, 50+) and exposure quintile, normalised to November 2022 (October 2022 in the 2025 versions). Supplementary: occupation-level long-difference regressions with controls, within-firm Poisson event studies with firm-time fixed effects, hiring and separation flows, CPS and ACS benchmarks.
evidence_offered: Headline 19%: a raw comparison of headcount indices, no model. 'Reduced hiring rather than separations' rests on Online Appendix Figure B.7 and Appendix K: a hire is a worker at a firm in month t but not t-1, a separation the reverse; both are cumulated over twelve months and divided by the cell's headcount a year earlier, measured January over January on the panel balanced from January 2018, comparing only the most exposed (Q5) and least exposed (Q1) quintiles by age group, shown as change since 2019. Finding: since 2022 both rates fell everywhere ('low hire, low fire'); separation rates for young workers fell at least as much in Q5 as in Q1; the hiring-rate gap between Q5 and Q1 young workers opened after 2022. Ageing out of the band and switching between quintiles were checked and ruled out (footnote 17). No numeric hiring or separation rates are given in the text, only the chart. A 'separation' is leaving the firm for any reason, so quits, layoffs and moves to non-ADP firms are not distinguished. Case for AI: gap kept widening after rates peaked; relative position was back at pre-pandemic level by November 2022; declines load on automating uses with an age gradient; sharpest in states with highest Claude usage (about -19% for the most exposed quintile in leading-adoption states); Census QWI data (Tucker 2026) show the same sign.
data_vintage: Three vintages. 26 August 2025: data through July 2025, headline 13% (regression). 13 November 2025: data through September 2025, headline 16% (regression). 'August 2026' revision released 12 August 2026 (PDF created 12 August 2026): data through June 2026, headline 19% (descriptive kept-pace), with 15% given as the same measure at the July 2025 vintage. The 2026 version also changed the data pipeline (new occupation crosswalk, imputed occupation codes) and the baseline month (November 2022 instead of October 2022). The essay should cite the August 2026 revision and say so.
figure_provenance: 13%: August 2025 abstract and conclusion; a regression estimate (12 log points) on July 2025 data. 16%: November 2025 abstract; same regression (15 log points) on September 2025 data. 15% and 19%: both from the August 2026 revision; a different, simpler measure. The trap: 13 to 16 to 19 is not one series. The like-for-like pairs are 13% to 16% (regression, firm controls) and 15% to 19% (descriptive, no controls). Writing 'the gap widened from 13% to 19%' mixes measures; the authors' own like-for-like statement is 15% to 19%. The regression measure behind 13% and 16% did not grow in the new pipeline: Appendix L puts the most-exposed-quintile within-firm estimate at -6.8 log points as of June 2026, or -5.3 (p = 0.26) under the original filters. Press coverage of the 2025 paper widely repeated '13%' and 'nearly 20% for software developers'; a web search summary of the 2026 release presents 13, 16, 19 as one sequence, which is the conflation to avoid. 'Nearly 20%' for young software developers is a 2025 figure (July and September 2025 data, peak-to-date, raw index) and has no stated successor in the 2026 text.
population_and_transfer: Working employees, not students: full-time US workers at ADP client firms, with 'young' meaning ages 22 to 25 (age, not tenure or job level). Covers all occupations; software developers are one case study among many and results hold when computer occupations (SOC 15-1) and tech firms are excluded. Transfers directly to the claim that fewer junior engineers are being hired in the US, with the limits that the sample over-represents larger firms, manufacturing and wholesale, and high-exposure occupations, and conditions on firm survival. It says nothing about skill formation or learning.
outcome_measured: Employment (headcount of worker-firm matches) by age and occupational AI exposure; hiring and separation rates; annual base compensation. Not job postings, not productivity, not skills.
limitations_stated: Authors' own, mostly quoted. Causality: 'this work does not estimate a causal impact of AI'. Education: estimates 'attenuate when controlling for occupational education levels, which may reflect either an alternative explanation or the very channel through which AI operates'. Pre-trends: 'more- and less-exposed occupations show some divergent trends that predate ChatGPT, particularly around the COVID-19 pandemic'; 'these patterns cannot be read as causal effects of AI'. External validity: 'the magnitude of the divergence appears specific to the ADP sample, but its direction is consistent' and the magnitudes 'urge caution against extrapolating them to the economy as a whole; a particular concern is that changes in the ADP sample might correspond to reallocation to firms outside the sample in equilibrium'. Selection: 'there may also be selection in which firms use ADP'; balanced panel conditions on firm survival; few firms under 10 employees. Hiring versus separations: pandemic-era differences 'indicate pretrends that warrant caution', and the flows 'are determined in equilibrium'. Pipeline: 'the firm fixed-effects estimates are more sensitive than the raw descriptive results'. Pay: base salary 'excludes bonuses, overtime pay, commissions, equity, and tips'. Forecasting: 'We do not make predictions about future impacts or claim that the trends we document will continue indefinitely.' Firm-level adoption cannot be studied because firm identifiers are anonymised.
counter_evidence: Inside the paper: the ACS shows a much smaller and statistically insignificant gap for 2022 to 2024 (-0.022 versus -0.132 in ADP), though the two agree for professional, information and financial services; the CPS is too noisy to say (23 to 48 young software developers sampled a month); the education control halves or more the estimate; the within-firm estimate for the most exposed quintile is no longer significant under the 2025 specification. Outside work the authors cite as finding different results: Lambert and Schindler (2026) find that accounting for work-from-home significantly attenuates the AI-exposure correlation (the authors' replication on ADP data disagrees and attributes the difference to data sets); Frank et al. (2026) document deterioration in AI-exposed jobs predating ChatGPT; Iscenko and Curto Millet (2026) and others raise interest rates; Humlum and Vestergaard (2025), Gimbel et al. (2025) and Eckhardt and Goldschlag (2025) are cited among studies 'finding a range of results'. These outside papers were not opened for this note.
alternative_explanations: Named by the authors: interest-rate rises from March 2022; unwinding of pandemic-era over-hiring in tech and knowledge work; the 2022 change to Section 174 R&D expensing, which raised the cost of software development; remote work and outsourcing; COVID-19 disruption to education and skill formation; shocks to college-educated labour markets generally (the education control); a general 'low hire, low fire' market that hits exposed young workers harder because their entry depends most on hiring and they enter at 22 or later (footnote 18); reallocation of young workers to firms outside the ADP sample; composition of ADP clients. The authors argue none is sufficient alone, and list 'AI, with COVID-19 education disruptions and work-from-home as other plausible contributors'.
verification_status: Checked against the primary source opened (August 2026 PDF and the 12 August 2026 news post): 19% wording and its construction; 15% at July 2025 vintage; the sentence attributing 13% and 16% to July and September 2025 data; data through June 2026; panel size; the Fact 4 hiring versus separations text and Appendix K definitions; causality statements; ACS comparison; education control numbers; Appendix L within-firm numbers; absence of any numeric software-developer figure in the 2026 text (searched the full extracted text). Checked against Wayback snapshots of the 2025 PDFs: 13 percent abstract wording (26 August 2025), 16% abstract wording (13 November 2025), data through July 2025 and September 2025, 'nearly 20%' for software developers in both, 6% decline, 12 and 15 log points. Not checked: values in Figure B.7 and Figure B.3 (charts not read), the Canaries Dashboard, and any of the cited third-party papers (Tucker 2026, Lambert and Schindler 2026, Frank et al. 2026).
relevance_to_essay: The strongest current evidence for 'fewer junior hires', and it supports the specific framing that the entry point is narrowing rather than existing juniors being laid off. It also supplies the mechanism the essay needs: AI substitutes for codified knowledge taught in formal education while experienced workers' tacit knowledge gains value, so the rung where tacit knowledge used to be acquired is the one being removed. It is silent on learning with AI and on training.
implications_for_training_design: None directly; the paper does not study training. Indirect only: the codified versus tacit finding (tacit knowledge 'acquired through practice, mentorship, and repeated exposure to real situations', per the news post) suggests in-house training for the juniors a firm does hire should target experience-based judgement rather than the documented, checkable knowledge AI already reproduces. The earlier November 2025 version also noted 'inefficient incentives to train entry-level workers who may move firms' as a reason firms cut entry-level hiring. Both points are the authors' suggestive framing, not tested findings.
open_questions: How far young software developer employment has fallen as of June 2026 (no number in the 2026 text; would need reading Fig. B.3 or the dashboard). Actual hiring and separation rates behind Fact 4 (chart only). How much of the gap is caused by AI. Whether the pattern holds outside ADP clients given the ACS discrepancy. Whether the missing hires are postponed, moved to non-ADP firms or gone. What the monthly Canaries Dashboard shows after June 2026.
